Here is the issue description:
# Bug report: multifmt slice uses wrong FP width for third operand
Hi,
the `fpnew_opgroup_multifmt_slice` uses the wrong FP width for the third operand.
AFAIK the third operand is only used by the `ADDMUL` opgroup, which expects that `operands_i[0]` and `operands_i[1]` have the FP format specified by `src_fmt_i`  and `operands_i[2]` and the result have the FP format `dst_fmt_i`:
https://github.com/openhwgroup/cvfpu/blob/5da3b411f3309d41b39dbc68da7449456f6be444/src/fpnew_fma_multi.sv#L36-L37
Accordingly, the `fpnew_opgroup_multifmt_slice` should use the width of FP format `dst_fmt_i` when assigning the individual elements of `operands_i[2]` to the lane instances. However, the width of `src_fmt_i` is used for all operands:
https://github.com/openhwgroup/cvfpu/blob/5da3b411f3309d41b39dbc68da7449456f6be444/src/fpnew_opgroup_multifmt_slice.sv#L181-L183
As a result, the third operand is incorrect for all lanes (except for the first lane), as shown in the following waveform. The first group of signals shows the `src_fmt_i` (which is `FP16`) and `dst_fmt_i` (which is `FP32`), as well as `operands_i[0]` (for reference) and `operands_i[2]` of the `fpnew_opgroup_multifmt_slice`. The elements of `operands_i[0]` which are 16 bits wide are correctly assigned to the individual `fpnew_fma_multi` instances (as seen in the signal groups below, which show the input operands of the first three instances). However, the elements of `operands_i[2]` which are 32 bits wide are not correctly assigned. The individual elements of these operands are surrounded by rectangles of different colors.
![fpnew_bug_annotated](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9446837/232724219-7daa7d8d-765b-4c12-9f0e-a2083a78c041.png)

<analysis>
The reported bug is that `fpnew_opgroup_multifmt_slice` slices all operands using `src_fmt_i` width, but operand 2 in the `ADDMUL` opgroup must be sliced using `dst_fmt_i` width. This affects lane-local operand alignment, especially for lanes beyond the first, because the third operand is packed in a different FP width than operands 0/1.

From the snippets, the primary faulty logic is in `src/fpnew_opgroup_multifmt_slice.sv`, specifically the lane input preparation in the generated per-lane block. The relevant issue is not just one assignment line: the whole lane parameterization determines the expected widths, and the conversion-specific override logic may also depend on the same slicing assumptions. Therefore, the inspection scope should include the lane parameter setup, the operand slicing loop, and the conversion override logic immediately following it.

The issue description also points to `fpnew_fma_multi.sv` as the semantic source of truth for how the three operands are interpreted: operands 0 and 1 use `src_fmt_i`, while operand 2 and the result use `dst_fmt_i`. This file should be inspected where operands are unpacked/classified to ensure the packing expectations match the slicer and to verify no similar mismatches exist in the input-processing path. The `trimmed_ops` generation and classification loop are especially relevant because they consume the lane-local operands and thus can reveal whether any other operand-width assumptions are encoded there.

In addition, the pipeline register section in `fpnew_fma_multi.sv` is structurally related because it propagates `operands_i`, `src_fmt_i`, and `dst_fmt_i` through the input pipeline. Although the bug likely lives in the slice module, the pipeline storage and forwarding path should be included in inspection to ensure the formats and packed operands remain coherent end-to-end and to catch any similar width coupling in the register chain.

So the key related locations are:
1. `fpnew_opgroup_multifmt_slice.sv` lane-generation and operand slicing logic around lines 146–193.
2. `fpnew_fma_multi.sv` input pipeline and input processing/classification logic around lines 140–199, especially the `trimmed_ops` handling.
3. Any nearby code in these files that establishes operand packing conventions or per-opgroup width assumptions.

These are the locations that should be reviewed for direct bug correlation, consistency, and any similarly structured width-selection logic.
